title: The Room of the Ninth Floor
premise: Paloma Halloran has spent five years in the mountain village of Vado Seco recording folk songs no one will sing twice, quietly documenting the strange noises from the abandoned ninth floor of the old sanatorium while telling themselves every sound has a mundane cause. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, Paloma realizes the village's 'found family' of survivors has been keeping something contained—and fed—by an unbroken ritual count that is about to fail. To save the family who took them in, Paloma must break their own rule of invisibility, lead the villagers in the forbidden songs, and finally answer the door themselves, trading their silence for the family's escape. In the end, the count stops, the ninth floor empties, and Paloma—changed, half-remembered by everyone they love—walks out of the sanatorium into a justice the law never could have given.
about_author: Petra Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist of Iberian oral traditions who spent a decade collecting songs from villages that no longer appear on maps. They write horror that treats folklore as a survival mechanism rather than decoration.

chapters.title: Songs No One Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Establishing the village, the recording project, and the rule: some songs may be recorded but never repeated. A grandmother cuts off mid-verse, terrified. Emotional beat: Paloma's loneliness and their comfortable self-deception that everything strange has an explanation.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma documents the derelict sanatorium from outside, counting the floors—nine where blueprints say eight. Nocturnal sounds: footsteps, a lullaby hummed in unison. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into obsession; Paloma begins lying to their own recorder.

chapters.title: The Halloran Rule
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashback. Why Paloma came to Vado Seco fleeing a scandal that destroyed their academic career; the village took them in without questions. Emotional beat: found family established—the Ortuña household feeds them, teases them, asks nothing. Staying invisible is their debt of gratitude.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Alternate POV: Tomás, the crew foreman. Machines bite into the sanatorium's foundations and strike a door—hinges on the inside, sealed from within, warm to the touch. Emotional beat: Tomás's pragmatic bravado curdling; he orders the crew to stop, then doesn't.

chapters.title: What the Door Wanted
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. That night the whole crew dreams of a corridor with a counting voice. Two men walk out of the village before dawn and don't come back. Emotional beat: guilt and complicity; Tomás hides the incident from the mayor, deepening the rot.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The village changes overnight: doors chalked with numbers, the grandmother finally singing a whole song—because it's a tally, not a lullaby. Emotional beat: revelation and horror; Paloma realizes the songs were containment, and their recordings may have thinned it.

chapters.title: Concilio de Medianoche
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, eavesdropping. The village elders convene: the door's unsealing has started the count, and the family—Paloma's household—are the hereditary counters. Emotional beat: Paloma learns their found family has been dying by inches for generations, one number at a time.

chapters.title: Marisol's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Marisol Ortuña's POV. The youngest counter explains the system to Paloma: each song sung buys a night; the count must reach a thousand or 'the room answers the door.' Emotional beat: Marisol's exhausted tenderness; she asks Paloma to leave before it ends. Paloma refuses.

chapters.title: Nine Floors Down
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, first entry into the sanatorium. The eighth floor doesn't exist from inside; the stairwell skips it. They find the sealed door and hear, behind it, a voice counting in their own accent. Emotional beat: the horror of recognition—something has been learning them.

chapters.title: The Two Who Left
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He finds the missing crewmen at the treeline, standing, counting aloud in unison, eyes on the sanatorium. He can't move them. Emotional beat: helplessness; Tomás finally goes to Paloma and confesses everything, forming the uneasy alliance at the story's core.

chapters.title: What the Recordings Did
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Reviewing five years of tapes, Paloma finds verses on recordings they never made—songs continuing after the singer stopped. Emotional beat: guilt made concrete; Paloma's archive is a wound in the village's armor, and they must decide whether to destroy their life's work.

chapters.title: The Burning of the Archive
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma burns the tapes in the plaza, an act of love against duty—their duty to scholarship versus their love for the family. Emotional beat: grief and liberation; the count slows, proving the songs can be redirected, not just surrendered.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Confession
chapters.summary: The grandmother's POV. She reveals the origin: 1938, the sanatorium's ninth floor, patients walled in alive during the war by villagers who chose their own families over the sick. The count is penance. Emotional beat: the village's guilt exposed; justice outside the law was never justice at all—only delay.

chapters.title: The Room Speaks
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The voice behind the door stops counting and starts bargaining: it offers Paloma the one thing they crave—recognition, a name spoken, a place in the archive of the world. Emotional beat: temptation; Paloma nearly accepts, and the near-miss costs Marisol a night of the count.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She tries to trade herself to end it, the way her mother did. Paloma physically drags her back from the door. Emotional beat: fierce, desperate love; the found family fractures over whether sacrifice is love or just another debt.

chapters.title: The Thousandth Number
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. The count nears its end; the village evacuates the valley road, and Tomás, choosing the village over his crew's paymaster, dynamites the excavation to buy time. Emotional beat: redemption; Tomás becomes a counter himself, an outsider joining the family.

chapters.title: The Song Paloma Wrote
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Realizing the entity feeds on inherited grief, Paloma composes a new song—uninherited, unowed—and teaches it to the village. Emotional beat: fragile hope; the count stutters for the first time in eighty years, and the door grows cold.

chapters.title: The Door Opens
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, climax begins. The door, sealed from the inside, unseals itself. What comes out is not a monster but a congregation: the 1938 patients, still waiting for someone to answer for them. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into accountability; the horror is human.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, climax. Paloma stands before the congregation and reads the grandmother's confession aloud, then their own—the recordings, the theft of grief, the five years of looking away. The village must hear its crime sung. Emotional beat: catharsis; justice delivered not by law but by witness.

chapters.title: The Cost of the Name
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. To close the count, Paloma gives the entity what it wanted: their name, freely spoken, entering its tally. The ninth floor exhales and goes dark. Emotional beat: sacrifice; the family watches Paloma's name fade from their memories even as Paloma still stands before them.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The village rebuilds; the sanatorium is demolished down to eight floors. Marisol remembers there was someone—sets a place at the table anyway. Emotional beat: mourning braided with warmth; found family persists past memory.

chapters.title: The Song That Remains
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, coda. Paloma, nameless and half-remembered, stays in Vado Seco as 'the archivist,' recording one last song—the new one, the uninherited one—sung freely by the whole village. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; love outlasting identity, and the count finally at rest.
